#### A Table of Contents

###### I Introduction

###### A Background

The control of vehicular platoons has attracted considerable attention since the mid sixties [2][3]. Recent technological advances in developing vehicles with communication and computation capabilities have spurred renewed interest in this area [4]-[12]. The simplest control objective for the one-dimensional (1D) formation shown in Fig. 1 is to maintain a desired cruising velocity and to keep a pre-specified constant distance between neighboring vehicles. This problem is emblematic of a wide range of technologically relevant, applications including the control of automated highways, unmanned aerial vehicles, swarms of robotic agents, and satellite constellations.

Recent work in this area has focused on fundamental performance limitations of both centralized and decentralized controllers for large-scale formations [5], [7], [9]-[12]. For centralized linear quadratic optimal control formulations based on penalizing relative position errors it was shown in [7] that stabilizability and detectability deteriorate as formation size increases. In [9], it was shown that merge and split maneuvers can exhibit poor convergence rates even upon inclusion of absolute position errors in cost functionals. In [5], it was shown that sensitivity of spacing errors to disturbances increases with the number of vehicles for formations with localized symmetric controllers that utilize relative position errors between neighboring vehicles. In [11], the analysis of [5] was expanded to include heterogeneous vehicles, non-zero time headway, and limited communication range within the formation.

The motivation for the current study comes from two recent papers, [12] and [10]. In [12], fundamental performance limitations of localized symmetric feedback for spatially invariant, consensus and formation problems were examined. It was shown that, in 1D, it is impossible to have coherent large formations that behave like rigid lattice. This was done by exhibiting linear scaling, with the number of vehicles, of the formation-size-normalized \(\mathcal{H}_{2}\) norm from disturbances to an appropriately defined macroscopic performance measure. In 2D this measure increases logarithmically, and in 3D it remains bounded irrespective of the system size. These scalings were derived by imposing uniform bounds on control energy at each vehicle.

For formations on a one-dimensional lattice, it was shown in [10] that the decay rate (with the number of vehicles) of the least damped mode of the closed-loop system can be improved by introducing a small amount of 'mistuning' to the spatially uniform symmetric feedback gains. A large formation was modeled as a diffusive PDE, and an optimal small-in-norm perturbation profile that destroys the spatial symmetry and renders the system more stable was designed. Numerical computations were also used to demonstrate that the spatially-varying feedback gains have beneficial influence on the closed-loop \(\mathcal{H}_{\infty}\) norm. The PDE approaches have also been found useful in the deployment of multi-agents [13], [14] and in coordination algorithms [15].

Even though traditional optimal control does not facilitate

Several recent efforts have focused on identification of classes of convex distributed control problems. For spatially invariant controllers in which information propagates at least as fast as in the plant, convexity was established in [18], [19]. Similar algebraic characterization for a broader class of systems was introduced in [20], and convexity was shown for problems with quadratically invariant constraint sets. Since these problems are convex in the impulse response parameters they are in general infinite dimensional. In [21], a state- space description of systems in which information propagates at most one unit in space for every unit in time was provided and relaxations were used to obtain suboptimal controllers. In [22], the optimal control problem for switched autonomous systems was studied and optimality conditions for decentralization of multi- agent motions were derived. In [23], convexity of the symmetric edge weight design for minimization of the mean- square deviation in distributed average consensus was shown.  

while references [18]- [21] focus on the design of optimal dynamic distributed controllers, we develop tools for the design of optimal static feedback gains with pre- specified structure. Even though the framework of [18]- [21] does not apply to our setup, we identify a class of convex problems which can be cast as a semi- definite program (SDP). Furthermore, we show that the necessary conditions for optimality are given by coupled matrix equations, which can be solved by a combination of perturbation analysis and homotopy- based Newton's method. We consider the design of both symmetric and non- symmetric feedback gains and show that departure from optimal symmetric design can significantly improve the coherence of large- scale formations.  

### B. Preview of key results  

We consider the design of optimal localized feedback gains for one- dimensional formations in which each vehicle only uses relative distances from its immediate neighbors and its own velocity. This nearest neighbor interaction imposes structural constraints on the feedback gains. We formulate the structured optimal control problem for both the single- and the double- integrator models. For single- integrators, we show that the structured optimal control problem is convex when we restrict the feedback gain to be a symmetric positive definite matrix. In this case, the global minimizer can be computed efficiently, and even analytical expressions can be derived. For double- integrators, we also identify a class of convex problems by restricting the controller to symmetric position and uniform diagonal velocity gains.  

We then remove this symmetric restriction for both the single- and the double- integrator models and begin the design process with a spatially uniform controller. We develop a homotopy- based Newton's method that traces a continuous solution path from this controller to the optimal localized gain. Along this homotopy path, we solve a parameterized family of the structured optimal control problems and obtain analytical solutions when the homotopy parameter is small. We employ perturbation analysis to decouple the matrix equations that result from optimality conditions, thereby rendering the unique optimal structured gain. This solution is used to warm- start Newton's method in order to efficiently compute the desired optimal gains as the homotopy parameter is gradually increased.  

In the second part of the paper, we examine how the performance of the optimally- controlled formation scales with the number of vehicles. We consider both macroscopic and microscopic performance measures based on whether attention is paid to the absolute position error of each vehicle or the relative position error between neighboring vehicles. We note that the macroscopic performance measure quantifies the resemblance of the formation to a rigid lattice, i.e., it determines the coherence of the formation. As shown in [12], even when local positions are well- regulated, an 'accordion- like motion' of the formation can arise from poor scaling of the macroscopic performance measure (formation coherence) with the number of vehicles \(N\) . Our objective is thus to enhance formation coherence by means of optimal localized feedback design. In situations for which the control penalty in the quadratic performance objective is formation- size- independent we show that the optimal symmetric and non- symmetric controllers asymptotically provide \(O(\sqrt{N})\) and \(O(\sqrt[4]{N})\) scalings of formation coherence. However, this introduces similar growth of the control energy (per vehicle) with \(N\) . We show that bounded control energy can be obtained by judicious selection of an \(N\) - dependent control penalty, leading to \(O(N)\)

**Conclusions:**

We propose an augmented hybrid 8DOF robot vision system called Microscope Information Processing System. This system is established on the genetic algorithm algorithm and the deep convolutional neural network detection for printed medical images. We hope that the microstructured handle information through the loading process of the feedback and the image quality of the three kinds of surfaces in the microstructured handle will allow printed medical images of complex contours and natural colors, thus enabling human-to-machine cooperation and building real-time processing technology for printed medical images. We also analyze the requirements of the workspace size and force transmission when constructing two fingers to print printed medical images simultaneously, and the suggestion and experimental validation results show the feasibility of the proposed tracing method. The overall feasibility percentage is recorded, and the proposed method can meet usability and efficiency requirements for printed medical images and handle rehabilitation under lost or damaged hands.

In particular, we consider  

\[Q(\epsilon) = Q_0 + \epsilon (Q_d - Q_0), \quad (11)\]  

where $Q_0$ is the initial weight to be selected, $Q_d$ is the desired weight, and $\epsilon \in [0, 1]$ is the homotopy parameter. Note that $Q = Q_0$ for $\epsilon = 0$, and $Q= Q_d$ for $\epsilon= 1$. The homotopy-based Newton's method consists of three steps: (i) For $\epsilon = 0$, we find the initial weight $Q_0$ with respect to which a spatially uniform gain $F_0$ is inversely optimal. This is equivalent to solving problem (SH2) analytically with the performance weight $Q_0$. (ii) For $0 < \epsilon \ll 1$, we employ perturbation analysis to determine the first few terms in the expansion $F(\epsilon) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \epsilon^n F_n$. (iii) For larger values of $\epsilon$, we use Newton's method for structured $\mathcal{H}_2$ design [29] to solve (SH2). We gradually increase $\epsilon$ and use the structured optimal gain obtained for the previous value of $\epsilon$ to initialize the next round of iterations. This process is repeated until the desired value $\epsilon = 1$ is reached.  

In the remainder of this section, we focus on the single- integrator model. In Section VI, we solve problem (SH2) for the double-integrator model.  

## A. Spatially uniform symmetric gain: inverse optimality for $\epsilon = 0$  

One of the simplest localized strategies is to use spatially uniform gain, where $F_f$ and $F_b$ are diagonal matrices with $f_n = f$ and $b_n = b$ for all $n$ and some positive $f$ and $b$. In particular, for $F_f = F_b = I$ it is easy to show closed-loop stability and to find the performance weight $Q_0$ with respect to which the spatially uniform symmetric gain  

\[K_0 = F_0 C = [I I] \begin{bmatrix} C_f \\ C_f \end{bmatrix} = T\]  

is inversely optimal. The problem of inverse optimality amounts to finding the performance weight $Q_0$ for which an a priori specified $K_0$ is the corresponding optimal state-feedback gain [34], [35]. From linear quadratic regulator theory, the optimal state-feedback gain is given by $K_0 = R^{- 1} B_d^T P_0$ where $P_0$ is the positive definite solution of  

\[A^T P_0 + P_0 A + Q_0 - P_0 B_2 R^{-1} B_d^T P_0 = 0.\]  

For the kinematic model (VP1), $A = O$ and $ B_2 = I $, with $ R = r I $, we have $ K_0 = r^{- 1} P_0 $ and $ Q_0 = r^{- 1} P_0 P_0 = 0 $. Therefore, the state penalty $ Q_0 = r K_0^2 = r T^2 $ guarantees inverse optimality of the spatially uniform symmetric gain $ K_0 $. The above procedure of finding $ Q_0 $ can be applied to any structured gain $ F_0 $ that yields a symmetric positive definite $ K_0 $, e.g., the optimal symmetric gain of Section III.  

## B. Perturbation analysis for $\epsilon \ll 1$  

We next utilize perturbation analysis to solve (SH2) with $ Q(\epsilon) $ given by (11) for $\epsilon \ll 1$. For small $\epsilon$, by representing $ P, L $, and $ F $ as  

\[P = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \epsilon^n P_n, \quad L = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \epsilon^n L_n, \quad F = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \epsilon^n F_n,\]  

substituting in (N1)- (N3), and collecting same-order terms in $\epsilon$, we obtain the set of equations (PA) with $ A_0 := A - B_2 F_0 C $. Note that these equations are conveniently coupled in one direction, in the sense that for any $ n \ge 1 $, $ O(\epsilon^n) $ equations depend only on the solutions of $ O(\epsilon^m) $ equations for $ m \le n $. In particular, it is easy to verify that the first and the third equations of $ O(1) $ are satisfied with $ K_0 = F_0 C = r^{- 1} B_d^T P_0 $ and with $ Q_0 = r K_0^2 $ identified in Section IV-A. Thus, the matrix $ L_0 $ can be obtained by solving the second equation of $ O(1) $, and the matrices $ P_1, F_1, $ and $ L_1 $ can be obtained by solving the first, the third, and the second equations of $ O(\epsilon) $, respectively. The higher order terms $ F_n, P_n, $ and $ L_n $ can be determined in a similar fashion. The matrix $ F $ found by this procedure is the unique optimal solution of the control problem (SH2) for $ \epsilon \ll 1 $. This is because the equations (PA), under the assumption of convergence for small $ \epsilon $, give a unique matrix $ F(\epsilon) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \epsilon^n F_n $.  

We next provide analytical expressions for $ F_1 = [F_f^{(1)}  F_b^{(1)} ] $ obtained by solving the $ O(\epsilon) $ equations in (PA) with $ r = 1 $, $ Q_0 = T^2 $, and $ Q_d = I $. When a fictitious follower is present, we have (derivations are omitted for brevity)  

\[f_1^{(1)} = \frac{n(n - N - 1)(4n(N + 1) - N(2N + 7) + 1)}{12(N^2 - 1)} - \frac{1}{2},\] \[b_1^{(1)} = \frac{n(N + 1 - n)(4n(N + 1) - N(2N + 1) - 5)}{12(N^2 - 1)} - \frac{1}{2},\]  

where $ f_1^{(1)} $ and $ b_1^{(1)} $ denote the $ n $ th diagonal entries of $ F_f^{(1)} $ and $ F_b^{(1)} $. From (12) it follows that $ f_n^{(1)} = b_{N + 1 - n}^{(1)} $ for $ n \in \{1, \ldots, N\} $. When a fictitious follower is not present, we have  

\[\begin{array}{rcl} f_1^{(1)} & = & (-n^2 + (N + 1)n - 1) / 2, \ n \in \{1, \ldots , N - 1 \}, \\ f_N^{(1)} & = & (N - 1) / 2, \\ b_n^{(1)} & = & (n^2 - Nn - 1) / 2, \ n \in \{1, \ldots , N - 1 \}, \\ b_N^{(1)} & = & 0. \end{array} \]  

To compute the optimal structured feedback gain for larger values of $ \epsilon $, we use $ F(\epsilon) $ obtained from perturbation analysis to initialize Newton's method, as described in Section IV-C.

In terms of the buffer queue, it is needed to ensure that at all times the new job will not run out of memory. Furthermore, the stability of the system should be guaranteed, that is, no instability of the queue or buffer will occur.

Now, the problem is how to allocate a virtual buffer of size 8 to each of N duration counters, so as to achieve the premise of stability. As shown in Fig. 3, one device buffer has an infinite number of periods, and traffic within the buffer is fair[12]. The arrival of jobs in each period follows a Poisson distribution. The arrival rate of the system at time t is equal to the product of the rate at time t and the number of the virtual device buffers at the same time t. Assuming the average number of buffers to be a constant $\hat{f_{0}}$ and $\hat{F_{0}}$, the queue length will change as is shown in Eq. (10). Since the process N has the finite buffer queue simulator, it cannot be calculated by $\hat{f}$ in (12), therefore we simulate the counter as an L-norm, not $\hat{f}$.

The arrival time of jobs in each period follows an exponential distribution, representing the arrival rate of jobs. The occupation time of devices has a certain mean value $\mu$, which is affected by the average workload $W_{n}$, which is expression (14). When the maximum capacity is set and the counter value $r$ is obtained, the occupation time of the counter's buffer $s_{t}$ is updated in Eq. (15) and 16. Due to the probability that the buffer overflow operation may occur, the larger the buffer control, the earlier the buffer overflow will occur, and thus the maximum buffer size should be set to be large enough.

### $C.~\text{Newton's method for larger values of } \varepsilon$

In this section, we employ Newton's method developed in [29] to solve the necessary conditions for optimality (NC1)-(NC3) as $\varepsilon$ is gradually increased to 1. Newton's method is an iterative descent algorithm for finding local minima in optimization problems [32]. Specifically, given an initial stabilizing structured gain $F^{0}$, a decreasing sequence of the objective function $\left\{J(F^{i})\right\}$ is generated by updating $F$ according to $F^{i+1}=F^{i}+s^{i}\tilde{F}^{i}$. Here, $\tilde{F}^{i}$ is the Newton direction that satisfies the structural constraint and $s^{i}$ is the step-size. The details of computing $\tilde{F}^{i}$ and choosing the step-size $s^{i}$ can be found in [29].

For small $\varepsilon$, we initialize Newton's method using $F(\epsilon)$ obtained from the perturbation expansion up to the first order in $\epsilon$, $F(\epsilon)=F_{0}+\epsilon F_{1}$. We then increase $\epsilon$ slightly and use the optimal structured gain resulting from Newton's method at the previous $\varepsilon$ to initialize the next round of iterations. We continue increasing $\epsilon$ gradually until desired value $\epsilon=1$ is reached, that is, until the optimal structured gain $F$ for the desired $Q_{d}$ is obtained.

Since the homotopy-based Newton's method solves a family of optimization problems parameterized by $\varepsilon$, the optimal feedback gain is a function of $\epsilon\in\left[0,1\right]$. To see the incremental change relative to the spatially uniform gain $F_{0}$, we consider the difference between the optimal forward gain $f_{n}(\epsilon)$ and the uniform gain $f_{n}(0)=1$,

\[f_{n}(\epsilon):=f_{n}(\epsilon)-f_{n}(0)=f_{n}(\epsilon)-1.\]

Figure 4a shows the normalized profile $\tilde{f}(\varepsilon)/\|\tilde{f}(\varepsilon)\|$ for a formation with fictitious follower, $N=50,~r=1,~Q_{0}=T^{2}$, and $Q_{d}=I$. The values of $\varepsilon$ are determined by 20 logarithmically spaced points between $10^{-4}$ and 1. As $\varepsilon$ increases, the normalized profile changes from an almost sinusoidal shape (cf. analytical expression in (12)) at $\varepsilon=10^{-4}$ to an almost piecewise linear shape at $\varepsilon=1$. Note that the homotopy-based Newton's method converges to the same feedback gains at $\varepsilon=1$ when it is initialized by the optimal symmetric controller obtained in Section III.

### _Spatially uniform symmetric gain_

For the spatially uniform symmetric controller with \(f_{n}=b_{n}=\alpha>0\), we next show that \(\Pi_{g}\) is an affine function of \(N\) and that, in the limit of an infinite number of vehicles, both \(\Pi_{l}\) and \(\Pi_{{\rm ctr}}\) become formation-size-independent. These results hold irrespective of the presence of the fictitious follower.

For the single-integrator model with the fictitious follower we have \(K=FC=\alpha T\) (see (5) for the definition of \(T\)), and \(L=T^{-1}/(2\alpha)\) solves the Lyapunov equation (14) [31, Lemma 1]. Since the \(n\)th diagonal entry of \(T^{-1}\) is determined by (cf. (8))

\[(T^{-1})_{nn} = n\left(N+1-n\right)/\left(N+1\right),\]

from (2.2) we conclude that the global performance measure \(\Pi_{g}\) is an affine function of \(N\), and that both \(\Pi_{l}\) and \(\Pi_{{\rm ctr}}\) are formation-size-independent,

\[\Pi_{g} = \operatorname{trace}\left(T^{-1}\right)/(2\alpha N)\] \[= \frac{1}{2\alpha N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}n-\frac{1}{2\alpha N(N+1)}\sum_{ n=1}^{N}n^{2}=\frac{N+2}{12\alpha},\] \[\Pi_{l} = \operatorname{trace}\left(T\,T^{-1}\right)/(2\alpha N)=1/(2\alpha),\] \[\Pi_{{\rm ctr}} = \operatorname{trace}\left(\alpha^{2}\,T\,T\,T^{-1}\right)/(2\alpha N)=\alpha.\]

For the formation without the fictitious follower, the following expressions

\[\Pi_{g} = (N+1)/(4\alpha), \phantom{.}\,\Pi_{l}~{}=~{}1/\alpha, \phantom{.}\,\Pi_{{\rm ctr}} = \alpha(3N+1)/(2N),\]

imply that, for the spatially uniform symmetric controller, the asymptotic scaling trends do not depend on the presence of the fictitious follower (derivations omitted for brevity).

### _Spatially uniform non-symmetric gain (look-ahead strategy)_

We next examine the asymptotic scaling of the performance measures for the spatially uniform non-symmetric gain with \(\{f_{n}=\alpha>0,\,b_{n}=0\}\). We establish the _square-root_ scaling of \(\Pi_{g}\) with \(N\) and the formation-size-independent scaling of \(\Pi_{l}\). Furthermore, in the limit of an infinite number of vehicles, we show that \(\Pi_{{\rm ctr}}\) becomes \(N\)-independent.

For the single-integrator model with \(K=FC=\alpha C_{f}\) (see (3) for the definition of \(C_{f}\)), the solution of the Lyapunov equation (14) is given by

\[L~{}=~{}\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm e}^{{-\alpha\,C_{f}\,t}}\,{\rm e}^{-{\alpha\,C_{ f}^{T}\,t}}\,\mathrm{d}t.\] (15)

As shown in Appendix B, the inverse Laplace transform of \((sI+{\alpha C_{f}})^{-1}\) can be used to determine the analytical expression for \({\rm e}_{{}^{-\alpha C_{f}\,t}}\), yielding the following formulae,

\[\Pi_{g}(N) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}L_{nn}~{}=~{}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} \frac{\alpha\,\Gamma(n+1/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(n)}\] \[= \frac{2\,\alpha\,\Gamma(N+3/2)}{3\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(N+1)},\] \[\Pi_{l} = ~{}\alpha,\] \[\Pi_{{\rm ctr}} = ~{}\alpha\,-\,(1/N){L_{NN}},\]

with \(\Gamma(\cdot)\) denoting the Gamma function. These are used in Appendix B to show that, in the limit of an infinite number of vehicles, a look-ahead strategy for the single-integrator model provides the square-root dependence of \(\Pi_{g}\) on \(N\) and the formation-size-independent \(\Pi_{l}\) and \(\Pi_{{\rm ctr}}\).

### _Optimal symmetric and non-symmetric controllers_

We next examine the asymptotic scaling of the performance measures for the optimal symmetric and non-symmetric gains of Sections III and IV-C. For the formation without the fictitious follower, we _analytically_ establish that the optimal symmetric gains asymptotically provide \(O(\sqrt{N})\), \(O(1/\sqrt{N})\), and \(O(\sqrt{N})\) scalings of \(\Pi_{g}\), \(\Pi_{l}\), and \(\Pi_{{\rm ctr}}\), respectively. We then use numerical computations to (i) confirm these scaling trends for the optimal symmetric gains in the presence of the fictitious follower; and to (ii) show a fourth-root dependence of \(\Pi_{g}\) and \(\Pi_{{\rm ctr}}\) on \(N\) and an \(O(1/\sqrt[4]{N})\) dependence of \(\Pi_{l}\) for the optimal non-symmetric gains. All these scalings are obtained by solving (SH2) with the formation-size-independent control penalty \(r\) and \(Q=I\). We also demonstrate that uniform control variance (per vehicle) can be obtained by judicious selection of an \(N\)-dependent \(r\). For the optimal symmetric and non-symmetric gains, this constraint on control energy (variance) increases the asymptotic dependence of \(\Pi_{g}\) on \(N\) to linear and square-root, respectively.

For the formation without the fictitious follower, the optimal symmetric gains are given by (9). As shown in (2.2), \(\operatorname{trace}\left(K^{-1}\right)=\operatorname{trace}\left(r\,K\right)\), thereby yielding

\[\Pi_{g} = r\,\Pi_{{\rm ctr}}~{}=~{}\frac{1}{2\,N}\operatorname{trace}\left( K^{-1}\right)\] \[= \frac{\sqrt{r}}{2N}\left(\sqrt{N}\,+\,\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\sqrt{2n} \right).\]

In the limit of an infinite number of vehicles,

\[\lim_{N\,\to\,\infty}\frac{\Pi_{g}(N)}{\sqrt{N}} = \lim_{N\,\to\,\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\sqrt{\frac{rn}{2N}}\frac{1} {N}\] \[= \int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{\frac{rx}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x\,=\,\sqrt{\frac{2r}{ 9}},\]

which, for an \(N\)-independent \(r\), leads to an asymptotic square-root dependence of \(\Pi_{g}\) and \(\Pi_{{\rm ctr}}\) on \(N\),

\[\Pi_{g}(N)~{}=~{}\sqrt{\frac{2\,r\,N}{9}}\,+\,\sqrt{\frac{r}{4N}},\;\;N\, \gg\,1\] (17) \[\Pi_{{\rm ctr}}(N)~{}=~{}\sqrt{\frac{2N}{9r}}\,+\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{ 4\,r\,N}},\;\;N\,\gg\,1.\]

Similar calculation can be used to obtain \(O(1/\sqrt{N})\) asymp

### _Discussion_

The study of dynamical systems with fictitious followers is still at an early stage of studying [21, 24]. One can find a large number of literature on this topic, e.g.,抛物抛物型Inline Dynamic Generation, for \(N=50\), \(I=1\), \(\ell=1\), \(r=0.1\), \(\epsilon=0.109\).

At the first preliminary stage (Fig. 7), we have established model theory and realized the required optimality condition, i.e., \(r_{1}>0\). The second stage (Fig. 7) allows for deviating from the theoretical and visual calculation of the optimal gains, so we incorporate the peculiarity of mixed reality. Thus it supports a more specific and convenient method. Combined with maximum oversight (Fig. 6), it created a debatable conclusion that the optimal gains of the feedback gains are high, though the optimal speed does not vary with additional initial speed, \(V_{\infty}\), which may be due to the limitation of the large-scale actuator modulation system (not studied in this paper) which has been researched in [25].

In the future, we will extend the system's synchronization control theory to study more general physical system models. This will increase the applicability of the insights obtained in this paper.

### _Conclusions_

We introduce a new family of asymptotically optimal controllers for multi-robot formation tracking. This approach makes the reward function based on a mixture controller approach a realistic task. In the future, it will be extended to the Dynamic Dynamic Mirroring (DDM) mechanism, which affects the overall dynamics of robots.

## VI DOUBLE-INTEGRATOR MODEL

In this section, we solve (SH2) for the double-integrator

model using the homotopy-based Newton's method. We then discuss the influence of the optimal structured gain on the asymptotic scaling of the performance measures introduced in Section II-C. For a formation in which each vehicle - in addition to relative positions with respect to its immediate neighbors - has access to its own velocity, our results highlight similarity between optimal forward and backward position gains for the single- and the double-integrator models. We further show that the performance measures exhibit similar scaling properties to those found in single-integrators. We also establish convexity of (SH2) for the double-integrator model by restricting the controller to symmetric position and uniform diagoal velocity gains.

The perturbation analysis and the homotopy-based Newton's method closely follow the procedure described in Sections IV-B and IV-C, respectively. In particular, \(F_{0}=[\alpha I\,\,\,\alpha I\,\,\,\beta I\,]\) yields \(K_{0}=F_{0}C=[\alpha T\,\,\,\beta I\,]\). As shown in [35], for positive \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) with \(\beta^{2}>8\alpha\), this spatially uniform structured feedback gain is stabilizing and inversely

## Appendix

### B. Gradient method for (SG)

We next describe the gradient method for solving (SG). Let us denote \(k=\lceil k_{1}\cdots k_{N+1}\rceil^{T}\). Starting with an initial guess \(k^{0}\) that guarantees positive definiteness of \(K^{0}\), vector \(k\) is updated \(k^{i+1}=k^{i}-s^{i}\nabla J(k^{i})\), until the norm of gradient is small enough, \(\|\nabla J(k^{i})\|<\epsilon\). Here, \(s^{i}\) is the step-size determined by the backtracking line search [32, Section 9.2]: let \(s^{i}=1\) and repeat \(s^{i}:=\beta s^{i}\) with \(\beta\in(0,1)\) until a sufficient decrease in the objective function is achieved,

\[J(k^{i}-s^{i}\nabla J(k^{i}))<J(k^{i})-\alpha s^{i}\|\nabla J(k^{i})\|^{2},\]

where \(\alpha\in(0,0.5)\). Note that \(J(k^{i})\) is defined as infinity if \(K\) in (7) determined by \(k^{i}\) is not positive definite. For \(Q=I\),

\[J=\frac{1}{2}\text{trace }(K^{-1}+rK)\]

\[=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{\gamma_{n}(\gamma_{N+1}-\gamma_{n})}{\gamma_{N +1}}+r\left(\frac{k_{1}+k_{N+1}}{2}+\sum_{n=2}^{N}k_{n}\right),\]

the entries of the gradient \(\nabla J\) are given by

\[\frac{\partial J}{\partial k_{n}} = r-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\left(\frac{\gamma_{i}}{k_{n}\gamma _{N+1}}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=n}^{N}\left(\frac{\gamma_{N+1}-\gamma_{i }}{k_{n}\gamma_{N+1}}\right)^{2},\] \[n \in\{2,\ldots,N\},\] \[\frac{\partial J}{\partial k_{1}} = \frac{r}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(\frac{\gamma_{N+1}- \gamma_{n}}{k_{1}\gamma_{N+1}}\right)^{2},\] \[\frac{\partial J}{\partial k_{N+1}} = \frac{r}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(\frac{\gamma_{n}}{k_{N+ 1}\gamma_{N+1}}\right)^{2}.\]

### B. Performance of look-ahead strategy

We next derive the analytical expressions for the performance measures \(\Pi_{g}\), \(\Pi_{l}\), and \(\Pi_{\text{ctr}}\) obtained with the look-ahead strategy for the single-integrator model. The solution of the Lyapunov equation (14) with \(FC=\alpha C_{f}\) is determined by (15). Since the \(i\)th entry of the first column of the lower triangular Toeplitz matrix \((sI+\alpha C_{f})^{-1}\) is \(\alpha^{i}/(s+\alpha)^{i}\), the corresponding entry of the matrix exponential in (15) is determined by the inverse Laplace transform of \(\alpha^{i}/(s+\alpha)^{i}\),

\[\alpha(\alpha t)^{i-1}\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha t}/(i-1)!.\]

Thus, the \(n\)th element on the main diagonal of the matrix \(L\) in (15) is given by

\[\begin{array}[]{l}L_{nn}~{}=~{}\int_{0}^{\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\alpha \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha t}\frac{(\alpha t)^{i-1}}{(i-1)!}\right)^{2}\mathrm{d}t\\ ~{}~{}~{}~{}~{}~{}~{}~{}~{}~{}=\frac{\alpha\,\Gamma(n+1/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}\, \Gamma(n)}=\frac{\alpha\,(2n)!}{2^{2n}(n-1)!\,n!},\end{array}\] (19)

thereby yielding

\[\Pi_{g}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{L_{nn}}{N}=\frac{2\,\alpha\,\Gamma(N+3/2)}{3\, \sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(N+1)}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{\alpha\,(2N+2)!}{2^{2N+2}N!\,(N+1)!}.\] (20)

A similar procedure can be used to show that the \(n(n+1)\)th entry of \(L\) is determined

\[L_{n(n+1)}=L_{(n+1)(n+1)}-\alpha/2,~{}~{}n=1,\ldots,N-1.\] (21)

Now, from (21) and the fact that \(L_{11}=\alpha/2\) we obtain

\[\Pi_{l}=\frac{1}{N}\operatorname{trace}{(TL)}=\frac{2}{N}\left(\sum_{n=1}^{N}L_ {nn}-\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}L_{n(n+1)}\right)=\alpha,\]

Similarly,

\[\begin{array}[]{lll}\Pi_{\text{ctr}}&=&(1/N)\operatorname{trace}\left(LC_{f}^{T }C_{f}\right)\\ &=&\frac{2}{N}\left(\sum_{n=1}^{N}L_{nn}-\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}L_{n(n+1)}\right)- \frac{1}{N}\,L_{NN}\\ &=&\alpha-(1/N)\,L_{NN}.\end{array}\]

Using Stirling's approximation \(n!\approx\sqrt{2\pi n}\,(n/e)^{n}\) for large \(n\), we have

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{L_{nn}}{\sqrt{n}}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{ \pi}}\sqrt{\frac{n}{n-1}}\left(\frac{n}{\ln 1}\right)^{n-1}\frac{1}{\operatorname{e}}=\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{\pi}},\]

where we used the fact that \(\lim\limits_{N\to\infty}(n/(n-1))^{n-1}=\mathrm{e}\). Consequently, \(\lim\limits_{N\to\infty}\Pi_{\text{ctr}}(N)=\alpha\). From (19) and (20), it follows that \(\Pi_{g}=(2/3)L_{(N+1)(N+1)}\) and thus, \(\lim\limits_{N\to\infty}\Pi_{g}(N)/\sqrt{N}=(2\alpha)/(3\sqrt{\pi})\). We conclude that \(\Pi_{g}\) asymptotically scales as a square-root function of \(N\) and that \(\Pi_{\text{ctr}}\) is formation-size-independent as \(N\) increases to infinity.
